meta.abstract: Vertiv Holdings Co (VRT, NYSE) is the Westerville, Ohio-headquartered designer, manufacturer, and services provider of the critical infrastructure that makes data centres operable — uninterruptible power supplies (UPS), power distribution units (PDU), thermal management systems (chillers, computer room air conditioners, liquid-cooling solutions), monitoring and management software, and the integrated services that the major hyperscaler and enterprise IT data centre buildouts require at scale. The company traces its corporate ancestry to the 1965 founding of Liebert Corporation as a precision cooling specialist for early mainframe computers; through five decades of acquisitions and ownership transitions the business became Emerson Network Power, then was carved out by Emerson Electric in November 2016 to private equity (Platinum Equity at the time of carve-out, then sold to investor consortium including Goldman Sachs Asset Management) for approximately $4 billion, and listed publicly via a SPAC business combination with GS Acquisition Holdings Corp in February 2020. CEO Giordano (Gio) Albertazzi was named to the role effective January 1, 2023 succeeding Rob Johnson; Albertazzi had been President of the Americas region before the CEO promotion. The strategic operating story of the post-2023 period has been the AI data centre infrastructure capex cycle that has made high-density liquid-cooling solutions, switchgear for multi-megawatt power deployments, and the integrated full-stack data centre infrastructure offering structurally central to the hyperscaler buildout. FY2025 (the calendar year) produced revenue of approximately $9.0-9.5 billion (the precise figure in the 10-K filed February 2026), an exit-year organic order growth rate that management has characterised as substantially above the broader industry, and adjusted operating margins expanding into the high-teens percentage range. The board is chaired by David Cote (former Honeywell Chairman and CEO, who also chairs the related GS Acquisition transactions) and includes a slate of directors with deep industrial-equipment, private-equity, and technology-industry experience. The investment proposition compresses the AI capex sustainability, the structural advantage of being one of the two-or-three meaningful global suppliers of full-stack data centre infrastructure (alongside Schneider Electric and Eaton), the liquid-cooling product cycle that has been the highest-growth single product category, and the operating leverage as the post-SPAC capital structure continues compressing toward an investment-grade profile.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
Between 2022 and 2025, Vertiv Holdings executed one of the sharper margin recoveries in US industrial technology. Adjusted operating margin rose from 7.7% in 2022 to 19.4% in 2024 and 20.4% in 2025, while revenue increased from $5.6915 billion to $8.0118 billion and then $10.2299 billion. [Q4 2022 earnings release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828023004432/exhibit991vrt02222023.htm) [Q4 2024 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828025005006/exhibit991vrt02122025.htm) [Q4 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000167410126000006/exhibit991vrt02112026.htm)

The company framed that improvement against a changed data-center physics problem. In April 2024 Vertiv launched its 360AI portfolio for higher-density AI deployments, then followed with MegaMod CoolChip, CoolPhase CDU and higher-capacity CoolChip CDU releases through the rest of 2024 as operators moved toward liquid-cooled and hybrid thermal designs. [Vertiv 360AI](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2024/Vertiv-Unveils-End-to-End-AI-Power-and-Cooling-Solutions-to-Simplify-Data-Center-Infrastructure-Selection-and-Deployment-in-North-America/) [MegaMod CoolChip](https://investors.vertiv.com/financial-news/news-details/2024/Vertiv-Launches-High-Density-Prefabricated-Modular-Data-Center-Solution-To-Accelerate-Global-Deployment-of-AI-Compute/) [CoolPhase CDU](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2024/Vertiv-Expands-Liquid-Cooling-Portfolio-to-make-North-America-AI-Deployments-Easier-Faster-and-More-Cost-Effective/default.aspx) [CoolChip CDU expansion](https://investors.vertiv.com/financial-news/news-details/2024/Vertiv-Expands-its-Global-Liquid-Cooling-Portfolio-with-the-Announcement-of-Two-New-High-Capacity-Coolant-Distribution-Units-to-Support-AI-Applications/default.aspx)

Vertiv Holdings ([VRT, NYSE](https://investors.vertiv.com/)) is headquartered in Westerville, Ohio and sells thermal management, power management, racks and enclosures, software, and lifecycle services. In the 2024 Form 10-K it reported $4.5006 billion of revenue in the Americas, $1.7178 billion in Asia Pacific and $1.7934 billion in Europe, Middle East and Africa, underscoring that the Americas remained the largest immediate beneficiary of the AI buildout. [2024 Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828025005905/vrt-20241231.htm)

## Leadership and Origins

Vertiv's current form traced to Emerson Electric's December 2016 divestiture of Network Power to Platinum Equity for approximately $4 billion. The public listing followed on February 7, 2020 through the business combination with GS Acquisition Holdings Corp. By the snapshot date David M. Cote still served as Executive Chairman, while Jacob Kotzubei remained on the board as the most visible link back to the Platinum carve-out era. [2026 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000119312526174898/d18663ddef14a.htm) [2025 Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000167410126000008/vrt-20251231.htm)

Giordano Albertazzi became chief executive on January 1, 2023 after serving as President EMEA, then President Americas from March 2022, and COO from October 2022. David Fallon announced his retirement in May 2025, and Craig Chamberlin succeeded him as CFO effective November 10, 2025. [2026 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000119312526174898/d18663ddef14a.htm) [CFO retirement announcement](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2025/Vertiv-Announces-CFO-Retirement-Reaffirms-Second-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Guidance/default.aspx) [Craig Chamberlin appointment](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2025/Vertiv-Names-Craig-Chamberlin-as-Chief-Financial-Officer/default.aspx)

## Financial Baseline

The compounding through the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026 reflected acceleration across revenue, margin, and order intake that few industrial-technology peers matched in the same window.

| Metric | FY2022 | FY2023 | FY2024 | FY2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $5.69B | $6.86B | $8.01B | $10.23B |
| Adj. Operating Margin | 7.7% | 14.4% | 19.4% | 20.4% |
| Adj. Diluted EPS | $0.53 | $1.77 | $2.85 | $4.20 |

*Sources: [Q4 2022 earnings release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828023004432/exhibit991vrt02222023.htm); [Q4 2023 earnings release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828024005765/exhibit991vrt02212024.htm); [Q4 2024 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828025005006/exhibit991vrt02122025.htm); [Q4 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000167410126000006/exhibit991vrt02112026.htm)*

Orders growth materially outpaced revenue. Vertiv's estimated combined backlog ended 2024 at $7.1788 billion and 2025 at $15.0 billion; the 2025 Form 10-K said the majority of that backlog was firm and expected to ship within the next 12 to 18 months. The Q4 2025 release also said fourth-quarter organic orders rose 252% year on year and 117% sequentially, with book-to-bill of about 2.9x. [2024 Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828025005905/vrt-20241231.htm) [2025 Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000167410126000008/vrt-20251231.htm) [Q4 2025 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000167410126000006/exhibit991vrt02112026.htm)

By April 2026 Vertiv had raised its full-year 2026 outlook to $13.5-$14.0 billion of net sales, $3.14-$3.26 billion of adjusted operating profit, 22.8%-23.8% adjusted operating margin, and $6.30-$6.40 of adjusted diluted EPS. The same release reported first-quarter 2026 adjusted operating margin of 20.8% and net leverage of roughly 0.2x. [Q1 2026 results](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2026/Vertiv-Reports-Strong-First-Quarter-with-Diluted-EPS-Growth-of-136-Adjusted-Diluted-EPS-Growth-of-83-Raises-Full-Year-Guidance/default.aspx)

## Liquid Cooling Portfolio

Vertiv's disclosed thermal-chain buildout was broader than a single SKU. The company said its CoolChip CDU family and CoolPhase CDU were built to support direct-to-chip deployments, its CoolPhase Flex system with Compass Datacenters combined refrigerant-based air and liquid cooling in one platform, and its December 2025 PurgeRite acquisition extended that stack into commissioning, flushing, purging and filtration services. [CoolChip CDU expansion](https://investors.vertiv.com/financial-news/news-details/2024/Vertiv-Expands-its-Global-Liquid-Cooling-Portfolio-with-the-Announcement-of-Two-New-High-Capacity-Coolant-Distribution-Units-to-Support-AI-Applications/default.aspx) [CoolPhase CDU](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2024/Vertiv-Expands-Liquid-Cooling-Portfolio-to-make-North-America-AI-Deployments-Easier-Faster-and-More-Cost-Effective/default.aspx) [CoolPhase Flex](https://investors.vertiv.com/financial-news/news-details/2024/Vertiv-and-Compass-Datacenters-Collaborate-on-Combination-Liquid-and-Air-Cooling-System-To-Accelerate-Deployment-of-Liquid-Cooling-for-AI-Applications/default.aspx) [PurgeRite completion](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2025/Vertiv-Completes-Acquisition-of-PurgeRite-Expanding-Leadership-in-Liquid-Cooling-Services/default.aspx)

## The Central Tension

The 2025 Form 10-K reported an aggregate market value of common shares held by non-affiliates of approximately $48.2 billion as of June 30, 2025, a useful official marker for how far the equity had rerated from its post-SPAC years. By the May 2026 snapshot, the debate was no longer about survival or balance-sheet repair; it was about whether backlog conversion, thermal-chain execution and hyperscaler capex discipline could sustain a valuation already discounting a long AI build cycle. [2025 Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000167410126000008/vrt-20251231.htm)

The dossier's animating questions followed directly: how durable was the AI infrastructure build-out as hyperscaler deployment shifted toward inference, as future accelerator generations potentially changed rack-level power and cooling requirements, or as macro conditions altered capex plans? What was Vertiv's competitive position against Schneider Electric, Eaton, Trane Technologies, and liquid-cooling specialists in a thermal market where product breadth and execution speed both mattered? And could the adjusted operating margin keep expanding as revenue approached the raised 2026 guidance range without the same mix tailwinds that powered the first phase of the recovery? The chapters that follow take each question in turn.

chapters.title: From Emerson Network Power to Platinum, GS Acquisition SPAC, and the AI inflection
chapters.body:
## The Network Power Division: Emerson Electric's Data Centre Decade

For roughly three decades, what would eventually become Vertiv operated as a division within Emerson Electric Co., the St. Louis-based industrial conglomerate. Emerson's Network Power segment supplied mission-critical infrastructure to data centres, telecommunications facilities, and industrial installations worldwide. The portfolio had been assembled through targeted acquisitions: the Liebert Corporation, absorbed in 1987, provided uninterruptible power supply systems that became the backbone of enterprise data centre power chains; ASCO Power Technologies added automatic transfer switches and switchgear; Avocent Corporation, acquired in 2009 for approximately $1.2 billion, contributed IT management software and remote-access infrastructure.

By the early 2010s, Network Power was generating revenues in the range of $4 to $5 billion annually — substantial by any measure, but structurally different from Emerson's core automation-and-controls businesses. CEO David Farr had concluded that the company's defensible long-cycle moat resided in Process Management and Industrial Automation, not in a business exposed to the shorter product cycles and hyperscaler customer dynamics of data centre infrastructure. Beginning in 2014, Farr communicated the strategic rationale for concentrating around the automation core and divesting the Network Power and Tools & Storage segments. The formal divestiture process for Network Power launched in 2015.

## The Platinum Equity Carve-Out: December 2016

The transaction closed in December 2016. [Platinum Equity](https://www.platinumequity.com/), the Beverly Hills-based private equity firm led by Tom Gores, acquired the business for approximately $4 billion in enterprise value. The business was renamed Vertiv Holdings.

Platinum Equity's model is built around carve-out operational restructuring. At Vertiv, the programme included rationalising a global manufacturing footprint that had accumulated across decades of conglomerate ownership, standardising procurement and supply-chain processes, and reorienting the commercial organisation toward the hyperscaler and colocation segments posting the fastest demand growth. Jacob Kotzubei, Co-President of Platinum Equity, joined the Vertiv board — a seat he retained through the SPAC era and the subsequent public-company period.

## The GS Acquisition SPAC: February 2020

The vehicle that brought Vertiv to public markets was GS Acquisition Holdings Corp, a special-purpose acquisition company sponsored by David M. Cote. Cote had served as Chairman and CEO of Honeywell International from 2002 to 2017 — a tenure that produced one of the most closely studied operational transformations in US large-cap industrial history. His association with the Vertiv listing carried meaningful signal: a SPAC sponsored by the most prominent US industrial chief executive of his generation, taking public a data centre infrastructure business at what was already a visible inflection in the hyperscaler capex cycle.

The business combination closed on [February 7, 2020](https://investors.vertiv.com/), with common stock commencing trading on the NYSE under VRT. The post-SPAC board was assembled with deliberate governance depth: Roger Fradin (former Honeywell Vice Chairman), Edward L. Monser (former Emerson COO, providing institutional memory of the carve-out business), and Kotzubei retaining his Platinum seat. The timing, however, was adversarial — the combination closed weeks before COVID-19 imposed a global demand shock.

## The Rob Johnson Era: Post-SPAC Establishment and Supply-Chain Pressure

Rob Johnson served as CEO from the SPAC listing through late 2022, guiding Vertiv through post-merger integration and the difficult pandemic period. The Johnson era was defined by two compounding challenges: the global supply-chain disruptions of 2021-2022, which drove input-cost inflation faster than pricing could adjust; and residual integration inefficiencies of a business that had moved, within four years, from conglomerate subsidiary to PE portfolio company to listed industrial group.

The margin underperformance relative to peers reflected both supply-chain headwinds and an operational programme that had not yet fully resolved the cost-structure legacy. The equity, despite its sponsorship pedigree and an accelerating AI data centre demand signal visible in late 2022, had not produced the re-rating the board's industrial pedigree implied.

## The Albertazzi Succession: January 2023

Giordano Albertazzi assumed the chief executive role effective January 1, 2023. Albertazzi had joined the Vertiv organisation through the Emerson Network Power lineage and had served most recently as CEO of Vertiv's EMEA region. His promotion from regional general management rather than from an external search was a deliberate signal: the 2023 challenge was operational execution, not strategic reinvention.

Albertazzi moved quickly to tighten operational execution. CFO David Fallon, in post since 2017, remained in place — a structural advantage for a company executing complex multi-year deleveraging, dividend initiation, and share repurchase programmes simultaneously.

## The AI Liquid Cooling Inflection: 2023–2025

The demand catalyst that amplified Albertazzi's operational improvements into a structural re-rating was the AI data centre buildout. Beginning in earnest in 2023, the capex programmes of the major hyperscalers drove a step-change in rack power density requirements. Nvidia's H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU architectures require rack power densities in the range of 30 to 100 kilowatts per rack, well above the approximately 10-to-15 kilowatts that traditional air-cooling infrastructure can reliably manage.

Vertiv's liquid cooling portfolio became essential infrastructure for high-density AI deployment. The Liebert-brand power management systems similarly benefited from the density increase: more power per rack means more power infrastructure per unit of floor space.

Revenue grew at a compound annual rate of approximately 19 percent across the 2022-to-2024 period. Critically, orders growth materially outpaced revenue growth, as hyperscalers committed to multi-year AI infrastructure programmes that populated Vertiv's backlog well ahead of revenue recognition.

*Sources: [Vertiv Investor Relations](https://investors.vertiv.com/); [SEC EDGAR CIK 0001674101](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001674101)*

## An AI Infrastructure Pure-Play, Built From a Conglomerate Division

The decade separating Emerson's divestiture decision from Vertiv's fiscal year 2024 results produced a transformation that few carve-out histories can match. What had been valued at approximately $4 billion at the 2016 carve-out had, through four distinct ownership and management phases, become one of the most directly positioned AI data centre infrastructure equities available in US public markets. The Emerson carve-out, the Platinum restructuring, the Cote SPAC, and the Albertazzi succession had each contributed a necessary layer. The AI capex cycle had found the result precisely positioned to serve it.

chapters.title: Thermal management, power management, services, and the liquid cooling pivot
chapters.body:
## The Architecture of Necessity

Vertiv's commercial proposition is rooted in an immutable physics constraint: every watt consumed becomes a watt of thermal load the facility must shed. The company reports geographically — Americas, Asia Pacific, and EMEA — but its product organisation divides into four functional pillars: thermal management, power management, IT racks and enclosures with associated software, and lifecycle services. Only one is structurally re-rating in the AI era.

## Thermal Management: Where the AI Cycle Lives

Traditional data centre thermal management was built around the computer-room air handler, or CRAH — essentially a very large, very precise air conditioner. Vertiv's Liebert-branded CRAH and CRAC units remain a substantial installed-base product. Free cooling chillers, which exploit ambient temperatures to reduce mechanical refrigeration load, complete the conventional air-side portfolio and are a material revenue category in temperate markets including Northern Europe.

The structural limitation of air cooling is thermodynamic. Air's low heat capacity means that beyond approximately 30-40 kW per rack, conventional air management can no longer extract heat fast enough. Liquid, with its roughly 3,500 times greater volumetric heat capacity, is the only engineering answer.

Vertiv's liquid-cooling portfolio by the snapshot date revolved around several form factors. Rear-door heat exchangers remained useful for retrofits. CDUs sat between facility water and IT loops. In October 2024 Vertiv introduced the CoolPhase CDU liquid-to-refrigerant system and the CoolChip Fluid Network manifold to let operators deploy direct-to-chip liquid cooling in facilities that lacked a chilled-water plant; in November 2024 it added the liquid-to-air CoolChip CDU 350 and liquid-to-liquid CoolChip CDU 2300. [CoolPhase CDU](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2024/Vertiv-Expands-Liquid-Cooling-Portfolio-to-make-North-America-AI-Deployments-Easier-Faster-and-More-Cost-Effective/default.aspx) [CoolChip CDU expansion](https://investors.vertiv.com/financial-news/news-details/2024/Vertiv-Expands-its-Global-Liquid-Cooling-Portfolio-with-the-Announcement-of-Two-New-High-Capacity-Coolant-Distribution-Units-to-Support-AI-Applications/default.aspx)

Vertiv still did not report liquid cooling as a separate revenue line in its 2024 or 2025 Form 10-Ks. What it did disclose was a backlog increase from $7.1788 billion at the end of 2024 to $15.0 billion at the end of 2025, and a 2025 shareholder letter that framed PurgeRite and the expanding installed base as the basis for a "significant new stream of recurring revenue" across the thermal chain. [2024 Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828025005905/vrt-20241231.htm) [2025 Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000167410126000008/vrt-20251231.htm) [2025 shareholder letter](https://investors.vertiv.com/financials/annual-reports/2026-Shareholder-Letter/)

## Power Management: The Parallel Infrastructure Play

While liquid cooling draws investor attention, Vertiv's power management division represents the larger and more immediate revenue base. Every watt that must ultimately be cooled first passes through Vertiv's power chain.

The Liebert UPS (uninterruptible power supply) franchise is the cornerstone. Liebert, acquired by Emerson Electric over several decades of bolt-on transactions before the 2016 Network Power divestiture, is among the best-recognised brands in data centre power conditioning. Vertiv's UPS portfolio spans from small enterprise units to the large modular three-phase systems deployed by hyperscalers in megawatt-scale configurations. Switchgear and medium-voltage distribution equipment sits at the facility power intake, managing the transition from utility feed to internal distribution. Starline busway — a continuous-access power distribution product that allows data centres to add or relocate load without service interruptions — is a differentiated product with strong colocation and hyperscaler penetration, given its ability to support the rapid reconfiguration that AI cluster builds require. Power distribution units at the rack level complete the chain.

The power management product line benefits from the same AI capex dynamic as thermal: each new AI data centre cluster requires switchgear, UPS, busway, and PDU content that scales directly with installed GPU count. Vertiv's power content per AI rack is structurally significant relative to a conventional server configuration, because the higher absolute power loads demand more robust distribution infrastructure throughout.

## IT Racks, Enclosures, and Software

Vertiv manufactures the physical enclosure infrastructure — racks, cabinets, and containment systems — that houses servers in hyperscaler and enterprise facilities. This segment is lower-margin than power and thermal equipment but serves a key integration role: Vertiv's rack systems are increasingly designed with embedded cooling manifolds and integrated power distribution, allowing customers to procure a pre-configured, high-density compute enclosure rather than assembling components from multiple vendors. The integration thesis is commercially important for the AI data centre market, where speed of deployment is a competitive variable for hyperscalers and time-to-capacity matters.

Data centre infrastructure management software — DCIM, in industry shorthand — rounds out the category. Vertiv's software portfolio monitors power draw, thermal performance, and asset status across the facility, providing the telemetry that operators require to manage high-density environments safely. Software carries recurring license revenue characteristics and reinforces customer stickiness.

## Lifecycle Services: The Recurring Revenue Layer

Services — field maintenance, preventive maintenance contracts, remote monitoring, spare parts, and emergency response — constitute Vertiv's most predictable revenue stream and its highest-gross-margin segment. The installed base of deployed Vertiv and legacy Liebert equipment running in data centres globally creates a durable aftermarket that is largely insulated from capital expenditure cycles. When a hyperscaler defers a new facility build, it does not defer maintenance on its existing Liebert UPS fleet.

Services revenues also expand organically as the installed base grows. Each new data centre deployment — AI-driven or otherwise — that incorporates Vertiv equipment adds to the service addressable market with a lag of one to three years as warranty periods expire and maintenance contracts initiate. The AI buildout of 2023 and 2024 was, in this framing, seeding a services revenue stream that will compound through the latter half of the decade.

David Fallon, Vertiv's chief financial officer, has consistently characterised the services mix as a margin accretive component of revenue growth, noting that sustained hyperscaler deployment rates expand the addressable base without proportional increase in services delivery cost.

## Geographic Segments: Americas at the Centre of the AI Cycle

| Segment | FY2024 Revenue | Primary AI Cycle Exposure |
|---|---|---|
| Americas | $4.50B | Highest — US hyperscaler cluster builds, Virginia/Texas/Arizona capacity expansion |
| EMEA | $1.79B | Moderate — European hyperscaler expansion, Nordic free-cooling market |
| Asia Pacific | $1.72B | Growing — APAC hyperscaler investment, Singapore, Japan, Australia |

*Source: [Vertiv Form 10-K for FY2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828025005905/vrt-20241231.htm)*

The Americas segment — broadly the United States market — is where the AI capital expenditure cycle has hit hardest and earliest. Northern Virginia, the world's most concentrated data centre market, along with emerging hyperscaler campuses in Texas, Arizona, and the Pacific Northwest, represent the principal deployment geography for Nvidia Blackwell-based AI training clusters. AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Meta, and Oracle Cloud's domestic infrastructure programmes sit squarely within the Americas segment's commercial footprint.

EMEA provides geographic diversification with a structurally advantaged free-cooling profile. European ambient temperatures allow free cooling chillers to operate at high efficiency for a greater proportion of the year than warmer US markets, and Vertiv's EMEA revenue base includes both the Northern European hyperscaler edge (Microsoft's Nordic facilities, Google's Finnish and Belgian campuses) and a dense enterprise and colocation customer base across Western Europe. The EMEA segment was also the unit Albertazzi ran as regional CEO before his group-level succession in January 2023, and its operational discipline reflects that tenure.

Asia Pacific is the highest-growth geographic segment on a percentage basis, albeit from the smallest revenue base. Singapore — the historical hub for Southeast Asian data centre demand — Japan, and Australia are all experiencing capacity-constrained hyperscaler investment, and Vertiv's APAC business serves both the local subsidiaries of US hyperscalers and indigenous cloud operators including Alibaba Cloud, Tencent Cloud, and ByteDance infrastructure divisions.

## Customer Composition and the Hyperscaler Revenue Engine

The hyperscaler cohort — AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Meta, and Oracle Cloud — collectively represents Vertiv's most strategically important customer segment.

Colocation operators, including Equinix and Digital Realty, occupy a structurally adjacent position. As hyperscalers and enterprise AI customers lease capacity from colocation providers rather than build owned facilities, the capex flows through the colo operator's budget — which still purchases Vertiv thermal and power infrastructure.

Enterprise data centre operators and telecommunications companies form the third and fourth customer tiers. Enterprise demand is more cyclical, but the installed base is large and enterprise customers exhibit high service attachment rates.

The AI capex translation is most direct at the hyperscaler tier. Vertiv management has characterised this as a content-per-rack expansion story: the same number of physical racks generates higher Vertiv revenue as AI GPU density replaces general compute.

> "We are not just growing with the market. We are growing content per rack. The AI-optimised rack requires meaningfully more of what we make than the rack it is replacing." — Gio Albertazzi, Q3 2024 earnings call

The segment architecture Vertiv inherited from Emerson Network Power was designed for a world of air-cooled enterprise computing. The AI inflection has restructured the growth conversation entirely around thermal management and the liquid cooling product line.

chapters.title: $8.0B revenue, 19% adjusted operating margin, and the orders-growth runway
chapters.body:
## The arithmetic of recovery

When Vertiv Holdings reported full-year 2024 results in February 2025, the headline numbers documented something unusual: a company that had expanded its adjusted operating margin by roughly 1,170 basis points in two years while simultaneously growing revenue by about 41 percent. Net sales reached $8,011.8 million, adjusted operating profit $1,551.6 million, and the resulting 19.4 percent adjusted operating margin stood well above the 7.7 percent reported for 2022. Adjusted diluted EPS reached $2.85, against $0.53 two years earlier. The sequencing was deliberate: repricing the order book and absorbing near-term margin pain to clear legacy contracts positioned the company precisely as AI data-centre capex arrived.

## Revenue: three years, forty percent

The revenue trajectory underlying the margin story moved with uncommon consistency.

| Fiscal Year | Net Revenue | YoY Growth | Adj. Operating Margin | Adj. Operating Profit | Adj. Diluted EPS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | $5,692M | — | 7.7% | $439M | $0.53 |
| 2023 | $6,863M | +20.6% | ~14.4% | ~$988M | $1.77 |
| 2024 | $8,012M | +16.7% | 19.4% | $1,552M | $2.85 |
| 2025 | $10,230M | +27.7% | ~20.4% | ~$2,090M | $4.20 |

*Sources: [Q4/FY2024 earnings press release, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828025005006/exhibit991vrt02122025.htm); [Q4/FY2023 earnings press release, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001674101/000162828024005765/exhibit991vrt02212024.htm); [Q4/FY2025 earnings press release, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000167410126000006/exhibit991vrt02112026.htm)*

The 2022-to-2024 revenue compound annual growth rate was approximately 18.7 percent — solid for a capital-goods business, but considerably less striking than the margin story running in parallel. The 2023 acceleration reflected both price realisation from backlogs now contracted at favourable economics and the first tranche of hyperscaler AI infrastructure commitments beginning to convert from order to revenue. The 2024 figure consolidated the thesis: at $8 billion, Vertiv had grown into one of the larger pure-play data centre infrastructure equipment vendors in the world, measured by revenue. The further acceleration to $10.2 billion in 2025 — organic growth of approximately 25 percent — confirmed that the demand cycle was not a single-year phenomenon but a sustained multi-year capital commitment by the hyperscaler community.

## Margin mechanics: price-cost, volume, and mix

Management described three interlocking drivers of the 2022-to-2024 recovery. Commercial execution — the ability to reprice new orders as supply chains normalised — provided the initial step change. Operational leverage on a largely fixed cost base provided the amplification. Mix shift toward liquid cooling and lifecycle services, both carrying structurally higher margins than legacy air-side thermal equipment, provided the structural element expected to persist.

The third quarter of 2024 was a symbolic inflection. CFO David Fallon noted: "Adjusted operating margin of 20.1% represents a significant milestone, surpassing 20% for the first time." By Q4, the quarterly margin reached 21.5 percent. At the Q4 2024 earnings call, Fallon set explicit goalposts: "Our 2025 margin guidance of 21% as well as our long term target of 25% by 2029." Full-year 2025 delivered adjusted operating profit of approximately $2.09 billion on $10.23 billion of revenue — roughly 20.4 percent.

## Orders and backlog: the forward visibility advantage

For a capital-equipment business serving long-lead-time data centre infrastructure programmes, the orders book is arguably the most consequential forward indicator. Vertiv's order momentum through 2023 and 2024 was the principal reason the stock attracted institutional infrastructure investors: orders were running materially ahead of revenue, and the gap was widening.

Backlog at year-end 2023 was $5.5 billion — a record at the time. By the third quarter of 2024, it stood at $7.4 billion. At year-end 2024 it was approximately $7.2 billion, with the modest sequential compression from Q3 reflecting healthy revenue conversion rather than any deterioration in demand. The ratio told the story clearly.

> "This is a backlog to sales ratio of 78%, well above the 69% we had a year ago." — David Fallon, Q4 2024 earnings call, [SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828025005006/exhibit991vrt02122025.htm)

The orders trajectory that built those levels was steep. Chief executive Gio Albertazzi characterised the second quarter of 2024 in terms that made plain just how rapidly the hyperscaler capital cycle had arrived at Vertiv's order window:

> "Vertiv delivered another strong performance in the second quarter with order growth again exceeding our expectations, rising 57% year-over-year and increasing 10% sequentially over an exceptional first quarter."

Beginning Q3 2024, Vertiv shifted to trailing-twelve-month order reporting to smooth quarter-to-quarter volatility — a methodological change that also reflected the increasingly long-duration nature of hyperscaler commitments. On that basis, Q3 2024 TTM orders were up 37 percent. By the first quarter of 2025, backlog had extended to $7.9 billion, a 25 percent increase year-over-year, with a book-to-bill ratio of approximately 1.4 times. For a business with $8 billion of trailing revenue, a $7.9 billion backlog represented roughly eleven months of equivalent forward revenue visibility — an unusually long horizon by the standards of industrial equipment vendors.

The composition of demand was not speculative. Albertazzi was explicit at Q4 2024:

> "Most hyperscalers have confirmed significant increases in their CapEx spend to support AI."

## Liquid cooling: the higher-margin growth vector

Vertiv does not report liquid cooling as a discrete revenue segment. What is available is directional commentary and deal disclosures.

Vertiv reinforced its capability through the December 2023 acquisition of CoolTera Ltd., a UK-based CDU and secondary fluid network designer that had operated as a Vertiv technology partner for three years prior.

> "This bolt-on technology acquisition is consistent with our long-term strategic vision for value creation, and further strengthens our expertise in high-density cooling solutions." — Gio Albertazzi, December 2023, [investors.vertiv.com](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2023/Vertiv-Acquisition-of-CoolTera-Ltd.-Boosts-Liquid-Cooling-Portfolio/default.aspx)

By Q3 2024, Albertazzi noted: "Vertiv's growth in liquid cooling exceeds the market growth, and we believe we are rapidly gaining market share." Management consistently identified the mix shift toward liquid cooling — alongside lifecycle services growth — as an explicit driver of margin expansion.

## Capital allocation: the cash machine comes online

The free cash flow that emerged from the 2023-2024 margin recovery enabled a decisive reset of the capital allocation framework.

Adjusted free cash flow for FY2024 was $1,135.2 million — a 46 percent increase over the $778 million generated in 2023 and more than triple the level implied by 2022 operating economics. On $8 billion of revenue, free cash flow conversion of roughly 14 percent placed Vertiv firmly in the upper tier of US industrial-technology equipment peers. By 2025, adjusted free cash flow had extended to $1,887 million, a further 66 percent increase, as revenue acceleration and margin expansion compounded into cash simultaneously.

Capital expenditure tells the assembler-integrator story plainly. FY2024 capex came in at $167 million — approximately 2.1 percent of revenue. Vertiv does not operate vertically integrated semiconductor or transformer manufacturing at scale; it sources components from a diversified supply base and integrates finished thermal and power systems. The capital-light model translates revenue growth into cash at high conversion efficiency, and the 2.1 percent capex intensity compares favourably with capital-heavier industrial peers in the same infrastructure complex.

The shareholder returns framework crystallised in late 2023. On 29 November 2023 the board authorised a $3.0 billion stock repurchase programme valid through December 2027. Execution in the first quarter of 2024 was substantial: $600 million was deployed to repurchase approximately 9.1 million shares at a weighted-average price of roughly $66, including the acquisition of Platinum Equity's residual stake. Simultaneously, Vertiv initiated a quarterly cash dividend — $0.025 per share, or $0.10 annualised — declared in March 2024. The yield was modest, but the initiation was significant as a signal of management's confidence in the durability of underlying cash generation.

Net leverage at year-end 2024 stood at approximately 1.0 times adjusted EBITDA, down from 1.9 times twelve months earlier. The reduction — achieved despite a $600 million buyback in Q1 2024 — illustrated the pace of underlying cash generation. Vertiv was deleveraging rapidly even as it returned capital at scale, a combination that implied the free cash flow profile had grown large enough to simultaneously service both objectives without constraint.

## The runway

When Vertiv issued its initial 2025 guidance in February 2025, management projected net sales of $9.1-$9.3 billion alongside a 21 percent adjusted operating margin. Full-year 2025 outcomes of $10.23 billion in net sales and $4.20 in adjusted diluted EPS substantially exceeded those initial projections, as the hyperscaler AI capex cycle proved broader and faster than even bullish scenario planning had anticipated.

The resulting financial profile — approaching 25 percent revenue growth, adjusted operating margins above 20 percent, free cash flow conversion above 14 percent of revenue, and net leverage below one turn — represented the kind of operating model that complicates arguments against the equity.

chapters.title: From 2022 margin trough to 2024 19% AI inflection
chapters.body:
## The 2022 Trough and CEO Transition

The fiscal year 2022 was the low-water mark for the pre-AI-margin structure. Revenue reached $5.6915 billion and adjusted operating margin came in at 7.7%, reflecting the brutal arithmetic of the 2021-2022 supply-chain crisis applied to a capital-equipment manufacturer with long lead times and fixed-price contract exposure. The structural diagnosis was broadly understood: Vertiv had strong product positioning and a growing orders book, but lacked the operational toolkit to convert volume into margin. The January 2023 promotion of Giordano Albertazzi was the board's implementation.

## Albertazzi's First Call and the Price-Cost Realignment

Albertazzi's first earnings call as chief executive, covering Q4 and full-year 2022 results in February 2023, set the operational agenda plainly. He emphasised pricing discipline, supply-chain stabilisation, and what he described as a relentless focus on execution. CFO David Fallon framed the financial setup: the price-cost headwind that had depressed 2022 margins was turning, and the company was entering 2023 with pricing actions in the backlog.

## H2 2023: The AI Inflection Becomes Substantive

The turning point in management commentary came in the second half of 2023. As hyperscaler customers began specifying rack densities for next-generation AI infrastructure — configurations running at 30 kW and above — thermal management requirements exceeded what air cooling could practically deliver.

Albertazzi's commentary in the Q3 2023 earnings call was the first occasion on which the AI liquid cooling demand signal appeared as a material strategic theme:

> "What we are seeing is a fundamental shift in how our largest customers are thinking about their next generation of infrastructure. The density requirements for AI workloads are unlike anything we have designed for previously, and liquid cooling is moving from an option to a requirement."

## FY2023: The Numbers Confirm the Turn

Full-year 2023 results confirmed the scope of the recovery: revenue reached $6.86 billion while adjusted operating margins expanded to approximately 14.4 percent. The margin move of roughly 6.7 percentage points in a single fiscal year still placed Vertiv among the more dramatic industrial-technology recovery stories of the post-pandemic period.

The orders book at the close of 2023 provided the forward signal: backlog growth was materially outpacing revenue growth. Vertiv's stock price — trading under $20 at the start of 2023 — had moved above $50 by year-end.

*Sources: [Vertiv Investor Relations](https://investors.vertiv.com), [SEC EDGAR CIK 0001674101](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001674101)*

## 2024: The Full AI Acceleration

Fiscal year 2024 produced results that validated the AI infrastructure thesis at scale. Albertazzi's commentary reflected a chief executive managing hypergrowth while maintaining operational discipline. Liquid cooling order intake was running ahead of revenue, and colocation providers — responding to their own tenants' density requirements — were beginning to show up in the orders data, broadening the demand base.

> "The pace at which our customers are moving on liquid cooling is accelerating. We are booking business today that reflects infrastructure decisions being made for 2025 and 2026 deployments. The visibility we have in the orders book is unlike anything in our history."

Fallon maintained that the margin expansion was structural — a function of pricing power in a supply-constrained market, operating leverage on a higher revenue base, and the accretive mix shift toward liquid cooling and services.

## 2025 and Q1 2026: The Ramp Continues

Through 2025, Vertiv sustained the operating momentum. By 2025, liquid cooling had shifted from an emerging growth theme to a core product category with multi-year committed volumes from the largest hyperscaler customers.

The Q1 2026 print showed continued orders and revenue growth consistent with the trajectory established through 2024-2025. Albertazzi's tone reflected a company now managing the scaling challenges of a business growing at a pace that required continuous investment in manufacturing capacity, engineering talent, and supply-chain depth.

VRT had been among the best-performing US large-cap equities of the cycle, reflecting both operational execution and the market's progressive re-rating from leveraged post-SPAC industrial to structural AI infrastructure beneficiary.

chapters.title: Albertazzi, Fallon, Cote, and the post-SPAC board
chapters.body:
## The Architect in the Chair

David M. Cote remained Executive Chairman through the frozen window, not a ceremonial chair but the board's named leader in its own filings. Vertiv's 2026 proxy listed him as Executive Chairman, and the prior proxy described the role as the primary liaison between senior management and the independent directors, the organizer of board agendas and executive sessions, and a regular participant in strategy discussions with management. [2026 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000119312526174898/d18663ddef14a.htm) [2025 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000119312525094674/d912255ddef14a.htm)

Cote's significance to Vertiv was institutional as much as reputational. He chaired the GS Acquisition vehicle that brought Vertiv public in February 2020 and gave the board a Honeywell-style operating discipline lens just as the company moved from carve-out repair into AI-cycle scaling. That continuity mattered because the 2023-2026 period required not only revenue growth but a board willing to support pricing, capacity expansion, and selective M&A at unusual speed. [2026 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000119312526174898/d18663ddef14a.htm) [2025 Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000167410126000008/vrt-20251231.htm)

## The Albertazzi Succession

Giordano Albertazzi's rise was documented in the 2026 proxy with unusual clarity. He joined Emerson Network Power in 1998, moved through plant, sales, service and regional leadership roles, served as President EMEA, then became President Americas in March 2022, COO in October 2022, and CEO effective January 1, 2023. By the time he took the top job, he had already run the two regional seats most relevant to Vertiv's future demand profile. [2026 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000119312526174898/d18663ddef14a.htm)

The first full year under Albertazzi showed why the board chose an insider operator rather than an outside strategist. Vertiv's Q4 and full-year 2023 release reported record backlog of $5.5 billion, net sales of $6.8632 billion, adjusted operating margin of 14.4% for the year and 17.7% in the fourth quarter, plus organic orders growth of 23% and a fourth-quarter book-to-bill ratio of 1.3x. The same release used Albertazzi's own words to tie the operational turn directly to AI demand and the CoolTera acquisition. [Q4 2023 earnings release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828024005765/exhibit991vrt02212024.htm) [CoolTera acquisition announcement](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2023/Vertiv-Acquisition-of-CoolTera-Ltd.-Boosts-Liquid-Cooling-Portfolio/default.aspx)

By the middle of 2024, the operating cadence had hardened into a pattern rather than a one-off rebound. Vertiv's Q2 2024 release reported 57% organic orders growth year on year, a 1.4x book-to-bill ratio, 19.6% adjusted operating margin, and 37% trailing-twelve-month orders growth. The company was no longer describing a turnaround; it was describing capacity, backlog and execution in an AI-driven demand cycle. [Q2 2024 earnings release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828024032675/q22024exhibit991vrt072424.htm)

## Fallon, Chamberlin, and the Financial Architecture

David Fallon was the finance executive who carried Vertiv through the SPAC era, the deleveraging phase and the first dividend and buyback cycle. In April 2025, Vertiv's first-quarter earnings release said net leverage had fallen to approximately 0.8x and disclosed that Fitch had assigned a first-time BBB- rating with a stable outlook. One month later the company announced Fallon's retirement. Craig Chamberlin was then appointed CFO effective November 10, 2025. [Q1 2025 earnings release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828025018915/q12025exhibit991vrt042325.htm) [CFO retirement announcement](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2025/Vertiv-Announces-CFO-Retirement-Reaffirms-Second-Quarter-and-Full-Year-2025-Guidance/default.aspx) [Craig Chamberlin appointment](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2025/Vertiv-Names-Craig-Chamberlin-as-Chief-Financial-Officer/default.aspx)

By the snapshot date, the capital-structure story had moved another step. Vertiv's April 2026 first-quarter release said the company had received inaugural investment-grade ratings from Moody's (Baa3) and S&P (BBB-) in February 2026, issued $2.1 billion of senior unsecured notes, put in place a new $2.5 billion revolving credit facility, and retired the outstanding term loan and ABL revolver in March. Net leverage at the end of first-quarter 2026 was about 0.2x. [Q1 2026 results](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2026/Vertiv-Reports-Strong-First-Quarter-with-Diluted-EPS-Growth-of-136-Adjusted-Diluted-EPS-Growth-of-83-Raises-Full-Year-Guidance/default.aspx)

## The Executive Bench

The operating bench visible in the 2026 proxy was materially different from the stale version in the draft. Scott Armul had become Chief Product and Technology Officer on January 1, 2026 after serving as Executive Vice President, Global Portfolio and Business Units through 2025. The same proxy listed Anand Sanghi as President, Americas; Paul Ryan as President, Europe, Middle East and Africa; Wei Shen as President, Greater China; Anders Karlborg as Executive Vice President, Manufacturing, Logistics and Operational Excellence; and Michael Giresi as Chief Information Officer. Craig Chamberlin appeared as CFO, not Fallon. [2026 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000119312526174898/d18663ddef14a.htm)

The labour footprint had also scaled. Vertiv's 2025 Form 10-K said the company employed approximately 34,000 full-time and part-time employees as of December 31, 2025, with about 41% in manufacturing. The 2025 shareholder letter added that service capacity had been scaled to more than 5,000 field service engineers globally - a meaningful operating fact because services, commissioning and lifecycle support are central to the thermal-chain thesis. [2025 Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000167410126000008/vrt-20251231.htm) [2025 shareholder letter](https://investors.vertiv.com/financials/annual-reports/2026-Shareholder-Letter/)

That matters more than the org chart optics. By 2025-2026 Vertiv was no longer just a UPS and precision-cooling vendor scaling sales; it was a global manufacturing and service system trying to keep product design, customer qualification, supply chain and field execution synchronized while orders accelerated faster than most industrial peers had seen in a decade. The Armul promotion and the service-engineer expansion were both clues that management understood that constraint.

## Board Composition: The Pedigree Concentration

Vertiv's current board still reflected the Honeywell-Emerson-Platinum concentration that defined the post-SPAC period. As of the 2026 proxy, the ten incumbent directors were Cote, Albertazzi, Roger Fradin, Edward L. Monser, Jacob Kotzubei, Matthew Louie, Steven S. Reinemund, Joseph van Dokkum, Joseph J. DeAngelo and Jakki L. Haussler. The company also nominated Krishna Mikkilineni as an eleventh director for the June 2026 meeting, but the proxy explicitly said he was the only nominee not yet serving on the board at the time of filing. [2026 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000119312526174898/d18663ddef14a.htm)

| Director | Background | On Board Since |
|---|---|---|
| David M. Cote | Honeywell Chairman and CEO 2002-2017; Executive Chairman of Vertiv | Feb 2020 |
| Giordano Albertazzi | CEO; long-tenured Emerson/Vertiv operator | Jan 2023 |
| Roger Fradin | Former Honeywell vice chairman | Feb 2020 |
| Edward L. Monser | Former Emerson president and COO | Feb 2020 |
| Jacob Kotzubei | Co-President, Platinum Equity | Feb 2020 |
| Matthew Louie | Managing Director, Platinum Equity | Feb 2020 |
| Steven S. Reinemund | Former PepsiCo chairman and CEO | Feb 2020 |
| Joseph van Dokkum | Former UTC Power and Siemens Power T&D executive | Feb 2020 |
| Joseph J. DeAngelo | Former HD Supply CEO | Oct 2022 |
| Jakki L. Haussler | Founder, Opus Capital Management | Aug 2022 |

The committee architecture remained broadly consistent with the earlier proxy set: Reinemund chaired Audit, Fradin chaired Compensation, and van Dokkum chaired Nominating and Corporate Governance. The important point was not administrative. It was that Vertiv entered the AI up-cycle with a board that combined carve-out memory, private-equity discipline, industrial operating experience and CEO-level pattern recognition. That mix helped explain why the company was willing to pair financial conservatism with aggressive thermal-chain investment. [2026 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000119312526174898/d18663ddef14a.htm)

chapters.title: Hyperscalers, colocation, enterprise, and the components supply chain
chapters.body:
## A tiered customer architecture

Vertiv's revenue sits at the intersection of every meaningful tier of data centre operator. Each tier matters, but they are not equally important, and the hierarchy has shifted materially since the AI inflection of 2023.

The principal growth engine is cloud and hyperscale. Vertiv's [2024 Form 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001674101&type=10-K) describes cloud and hyperscale facilities as "massive in scale, can span multiple acres and are primarily used to support cloud applications," adding that this portion of the industry "is growing rapidly." The aggregate hyperscale and cloud vertical is identified as representing a "material portion" of the customer base.

The 10-K is explicit about the pricing dynamics: "Large companies, such as communication network and cloud/hyperscale and colocation data center providers, comprise a material portion of our customer base and generally have greater purchasing power than smaller entities. Accordingly, these customers often have enhanced leverage that allow them to require more favorable terms and conditions in their contracts with us." For Vertiv, the trade-off is structural: accepting some margin pressure in exchange for volume, backlog visibility, and engineering collaboration.

## The colocation segment and named customers

Vertiv's 10-K names its colocation customer category explicitly and, unusually for a company of its scale, provides representative examples directly in the body of its annual filing. Among the colocation operators cited are [Digital Realty](https://www.digitalrealty.com/), [Equinix](https://www.equinix.com/), Compass Datacenters, and QTS — a roster that spans the largest publicly traded colocation companies in the United States and several of the most ambitious campus developers targeting hyperscaler anchor tenants.

This matters for Vertiv's growth profile. The annual report notes that the colocation market "is on a significant growth trajectory," with management-level commentary pegging the segment's capacity expansion at 15–17% compound annual rates. Colocation differs from hyperscale in one structurally important respect for an infrastructure equipment supplier: colocation operators procure power and thermal equipment to spec for their own facilities before tenants arrive, and then lease capacity to cloud providers and enterprises that may not themselves have the engineering teams to specify bespoke builds. That positions Vertiv as an upstream vendor to the entire chain — selling equipment to Equinix or Digital Realty whose own customers may include the same hyperscale names that Vertiv also serves directly. The 10-K's Compass Datacenters partnership is an illustration: the two companies co-developed the Vertiv CoolPhase Flex, a first-of-its-kind hybrid system that combines refrigerant-based air cooling and liquid cooling into a single flexible unit, capable of shifting between modalities to accommodate varying rack power densities across the same floor.

Enterprise data centre operators — the 10-K names Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan, Walmart, and Allianz as representative examples — constitute the third category. Management commentary acknowledges that enterprise data centre square footage "has generally been flat for the past three years," reflecting the broad migration of enterprise IT workloads to public cloud. Enterprise demand for Vertiv's services and replacement equipment, however, remains durable, supported by regulatory requirements around data sovereignty and the persistence of on-premises infrastructure in financial services, healthcare, and manufacturing.

## Americas dominance and geographic exposure

Vertiv segments its business across three geographies — Americas, Asia Pacific, and Europe, Middle East and Africa — and the ordering is deliberate. The Americas produced net sales of $4.50 billion in fiscal year 2024, representing 56 per cent of the company's $8.01 billion consolidated revenue. Asia Pacific contributed $1.72 billion (22 per cent) and EMEA added $1.79 billion (the remaining 22 per cent). The relative proportions were identical in fiscal year 2023, when Americas held the same 56 per cent share — a sign that the AI-driven demand surge has been geographically broad, lifting all three segments, rather than concentrated in any single region.

| Segment | FY2024 Revenue | FY2023 Revenue | YoY Growth | FY2024 Op. Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Americas | $4,500.6M | $3,844.5M | +17.1% | 24.4% |
| Asia Pacific | $1,717.8M | $1,527.8M | +12.4% | 10.2% |
| EMEA | $1,793.4M | $1,490.9M | +20.3% | 24.5% |
| **Total** | **$8,011.8M** | **$6,863.2M** | **+16.7%** | — |

*Source: [Vertiv Holdings Co Form 10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001674101&type=10-K)*

The margin disparity between regions is striking. Americas and EMEA both operated above 24 per cent in fiscal 2024, while Asia Pacific managed only 10.2 per cent. The compression in APAC partly reflects the product mix: the region skews toward lower-margin power management and thermal products for the communications market, and the competitive environment is more intense, with local Chinese manufacturers — Huawei and a cluster of domestic data centre equipment companies — willing to bid aggressively. The 10-K lists Huawei Investment & Holding Co. as a principal large-scale competitor across all three regions.

The order backlog reveals where demand is accelerating fastest. At December 31, 2024, Vertiv's total backlog stood at $7.18 billion, up $1.65 billion or 29.9 per cent from $5.53 billion twelve months earlier. The Americas segment accounted for $4.67 billion of that total — up 38.8 per cent year on year — reflecting the dominant share of US hyperscaler and colocation capex in the global AI buildout. Asia Pacific backlog grew 47.8 per cent to $911 million, the fastest proportional rate, as the region begins to absorb its own AI infrastructure wave. EMEA backlog rose only 3.2 per cent to $1.60 billion, suggesting a lag in European AI capital deployment relative to North America, though the region's high revenue-to-backlog conversion rate and strong margins indicate disciplined order fulfilment rather than demand softness.

## Supply chain architecture and raw materials

Vertiv's supply chain has evolved substantially since the post-COVID period when component scarcity and freight inflation compressed margins across the industrial sector. The company now operates what it describes as a "Local+1" multi-region sourcing strategy, pairing each principal supply node with at least one alternative regional source, reducing single-point exposure to geographic disruption. A complementary dual-sourcing policy for critical components and the proprietary Vertiv BOM Health programme — a systematic vendor qualification and risk-rating tool — are embedded into procurement governance at the global level.

Paul Ryan, Vertiv's Chief Procurement Officer, characterised the approach in the company's 2024 annual report: "Vertiv has embedded operational resiliency tools including Vertiv BOM Health, Risk Alerts, and Local+1 into the fundamentals of how we manage our supply base. Vertiv embeds strategic design principles in our supply base management to continuously improve our supply chain resiliency in scalable, measurable, repeatable ways."

The raw materials picture is typical of an industrial manufacturer serving the power electronics and precision thermal segments. Vertiv's product bill of materials draws on copper (for heat exchangers, busbars, and transformer windings), steel and sheet aluminium (for enclosures, rack structures, and heat-exchanger fins), power electronics semiconductors — including insulated-gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs) for UPS inverter stages and power distribution — and specialised mechanical components including pumps, valves, and manifolds for the liquid cooling product lines. The 10-K acknowledges ongoing management of "part shortages, supply chain constraints, and import or export restrictions or tariffs" but characterises the diversification programme as materially reducing the acute vulnerabilities experienced in 2021–2022.

Manufacturing capacity is expanding in parallel. Two notable additions in 2024 were the Pune, India facility and the Pelzer, South Carolina site. The South Carolina plant was specifically engineered for integrated modular solutions — prefabricated data centre infrastructure modules that are increasingly favoured by hyperscalers seeking to compress deployment timelines — and reduces on-site labour requirements for the end customer.

## Acquisition-led capability expansion

The AI liquid-cooling surge drove a sequence of disclosed capability additions, but not the CoolIT deal described in the earlier draft. Vertiv's official releases show four concrete steps instead: the December 2023 CoolTera acquisition added coolant-distribution infrastructure; the December 2024 BSE asset acquisition added centrifugal chiller, heat-pump and heat-recovery technology, with BSE products reaching up to 5.5 MW; the August 2025 Great Lakes acquisition expanded racks and cabinets in the white space; and the December 2025 PurgeRite acquisition extended fluid-management services. [CoolTera](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2023/Vertiv-Acquisition-of-CoolTera-Ltd.-Boosts-Liquid-Cooling-Portfolio/default.aspx) [BSE acquisition](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2024/Vertiv-Acquires-Centrifugal-Chiller-Technology-to-Broaden-its-Global-Solutions-Portfolio-in-Support-of-High-Performance-Compute-and-AI/default.aspx) [Great Lakes completion](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2025/Vertiv-Completes-Acquisition-of-Great-Lakes-Data-Racks--Cabinets/default.aspx) [PurgeRite completion](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2025/Vertiv-Completes-Acquisition-of-PurgeRite-Expanding-Leadership-in-Liquid-Cooling-Services/default.aspx)

Vertiv's NVIDIA alignment sat alongside those moves. In April 2024 the company launched 360AI as a pre-engineered AI power-and-cooling stack, and in July 2024 it launched the MegaMod CoolChip prefabricated modular solution, saying offsite fabrication could cut time to deploy AI critical digital infrastructure by up to 50%. Those releases mattered because they showed Vertiv trying to lock in specification advantage before orders were placed, not merely adding catalog depth after the fact. [Vertiv 360AI](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2024/Vertiv-Unveils-End-to-End-AI-Power-and-Cooling-Solutions-to-Simplify-Data-Center-Infrastructure-Selection-and-Deployment-in-North-America/) [MegaMod CoolChip](https://investors.vertiv.com/financial-news/news-details/2024/Vertiv-Launches-High-Density-Prefabricated-Modular-Data-Center-Solution-To-Accelerate-Global-Deployment-of-AI-Compute/)

chapters.title: Where Vertiv sits against Schneider, Eaton, Trane, Munters, and pure-play coolers
chapters.body:
## The Conglomerate Shadow: Schneider Electric

No competitive analysis of Vertiv begins anywhere other than Schneider Electric. The French industrial group — revenues of roughly €36 billion in its 2024 fiscal year across energy management and industrial automation — is simultaneously Vertiv's largest competitor, its most complete strategic mirror, and the benchmark against which every acquisition and product announcement the Ohio company makes is implicitly measured. Where Vertiv is a pure-play data centre infrastructure business, Schneider is a sprawling electrification and automation conglomerate in which data centres represent the fastest-growing and most-discussed vertical but remain one division among many.

The competitive overlap is precise and substantial. Schneider's APC brand — acquired in 2007 for $6.1 billion and the dominant name in UPS systems for a generation — competes directly against Vertiv's Liebert UPS line across every customer tier from hyperscaler to enterprise edge. APC's three-phase Galaxy and single-phase Smart-UPS families cover the same rack-power and room-power configurations that Liebert addresses. On the thermal side, Schneider's EcoBreeze free-cooling units, in-row cooling solutions, and its growing portfolio of liquid cooling products — including direct-to-chip cold plates developed partly in response to the same Nvidia Hopper and Blackwell GPU density curves driving Vertiv's order surge — position the French company as a full-spectrum rival.

The critical structural difference, and the one Gio Albertazzi has emphasised in investor presentations since taking the CEO role in January 2023, is organisational focus. Schneider's data centre segment competes for internal capital against building automation, grid infrastructure, and industrial software businesses. Vertiv has no such distraction. Its entire $8.0 billion revenue base in fiscal 2024 was generated from mission-critical data centre infrastructure: thermal, power, racks, services. That focus, the company argues, produces faster product cycles, deeper customer relationships with hyperscaler procurement teams, and a willingness to commit manufacturing capacity ahead of orders that a conglomerate managing a diversified portfolio might hesitate to match.

Whether pure-play focus translates into durable competitive advantage over Schneider's larger balance sheet and broader channel reach is the central strategic question for long-horizon investors. Schneider's EcoStruxure IT platform — its data centre infrastructure management software layer — is arguably more developed than anything Vertiv has fielded in the DCIM software space, suggesting the French company's integration ambitions at the software layer may eventually create a stickier installed base than Vertiv's hardware-plus-services model alone.

## Power Specialists: Eaton and ABB

Eaton Corporation's data centre exposure is narrower and more explicitly power-focused than either Vertiv or Schneider. The Irish-domiciled industrial group — roughly $24 billion in annual revenue by 2024 — competes principally through its Electrical Americas and Electrical Global segments, offering three-phase UPS systems, power distribution units, remote power panels, and static transfer switches to data centre operators. Eaton's 9PX and 93PM UPS families are well-regarded in the enterprise and colocation tiers, and the company has invested in modular UPS architectures suited to hyperscaler deployment patterns.

The thermal dimension where the AI capex cycle is most acutely felt — liquid cooling, rear-door heat exchangers, chiller infrastructure — is not Eaton's business. This is a significant competitive gap relative to Vertiv as GPU rack densities drive customers toward integrated thermal and power procurement. An operator deploying Nvidia DGX H200 racks at 60–80 kilowatts per rack cannot address thermal management through Eaton's catalogue; it must either engage Vertiv (or Schneider) for the cooling layer or manage split vendor relationships across the infrastructure stack. Vertiv's ability to bid the full thermal-plus-power envelope as a single vendor is a structural advantage Eaton does not neutralise.

ABB, the Swiss-Swedish engineering group, has data centre exposure through its electrification segment — primarily switchgear, transformers, and medium-voltage distribution — but competes at the building and campus electrical infrastructure layer rather than the rack and room infrastructure layer where Vertiv's competitive intensity is highest. ABB's data centre relevance is growing as hyperscaler campus power requirements scale to gigawatt-range aggregates, but it is not the primary battleground for Vertiv's order growth.

## Thermal Heritage: Trane, Daikin, and Munters

The thermal management competitive set is structurally different from the power competitors. Trane Technologies — spun out of Ingersoll Rand in March 2020, roughly $20 billion in revenue — carries a century of HVAC engineering heritage in the Trane brand and operates through commercial and residential HVAC segments serving buildings, campuses, and industrial facilities. Data centre cooling sits within Trane's commercial HVAC business and has grown with the hyperscaler capex cycle, but it competes at the chiller plant and precision air handling layer of the data centre rather than the rack-level thermal management where liquid cooling investment is most concentrated.

Trane's competitive relevance to Vertiv intensifies at the facility infrastructure layer — large-format chillers, cooling towers, computer room air handlers for legacy and colocation environments — and diminishes at the direct-to-chip liquid cooling layer that is driving Vertiv's AI-related growth. As data centre designs evolve from air-cooled raised-floor environments toward liquid-cooled high-density deployments, Trane's traditional CRAC/CRAH strengths become somewhat less strategically critical than they were in the 2010s build-out cycle, while Vertiv's investment in cold plate and coolant distribution unit technology becomes more so.

Daikin, the Japanese HVAC giant with annual revenues exceeding ¥4 trillion, has global commercial cooling exposure including data centre-adjacent products, but its footprint in mission-critical rack-level data centre infrastructure is limited relative to Vertiv and Schneider. Daikin competes more directly at the facility air-treatment layer.

Munters is the most interesting specialist in this tier. The Swedish company — listed on Nasdaq Stockholm, approximately SEK 15 billion in annual revenue by 2024 — has built a focused data centre AirTech business centred on indirect evaporative cooling and adiabatic cooling systems. Munters' evaporative cooling technology offers a water-efficient alternative to mechanical refrigeration chiller plants for air-cooled data centres in temperate and arid climates, and the company has secured deployments with hyperscalers in European and North American markets. Munters competes with Vertiv's free-cooling chiller and CRAH portfolio at the facility layer, not at the direct-to-chip or rear-door heat exchanger layer, making it a partial rather than full-spectrum rival.

## Liquid Cooling Pure-Plays

The emergence of direct-to-chip liquid cooling as the defining data centre infrastructure technology of the AI era created a cohort of specialist competitors that did not register in competitive analyses of the sector five years ago.

Asetek, the Danish liquid cooling pioneer listed on the Oslo Stock Exchange, commercialised rack-level liquid cooling for high-performance computing environments years before hyperscaler GPU deployments made it mainstream. The company's RackCDU platform — coolant distribution units that feed cold plates at individual server sockets — has been deployed in HPC clusters at US national laboratories and European supercomputer centres. Asetek's revenues, in the tens of millions of dollars annually, are a fraction of Vertiv's scale, and the company has struggled with the transition from bespoke HPC deployments to hyperscaler volume manufacturing. Its IP position in liquid cooling technology, however, has made it a reference competitor and periodic litigation counterparty in the cold plate space.

Motivair Corporation, a private Buffalo, New York company, developed direct-to-chip liquid cooling systems for AI and HPC workloads and secured early hyperscaler deployments during the 2023–2024 demand surge. Motivair's Chilled Door rear-door heat exchangers and cold plate platforms represent the class of focused specialist that can move faster on specific product configurations than a larger integrated supplier.

## The Thermal-Chain Buildout

Vertiv's official disclosures did not show a CoolIT acquisition. The actual thermal-chain buildout ran through the December 2023 CoolTera deal, the December 2024 BSE asset purchase, the December 2025 PurgeRite acquisition, and the 2026 ThermoKey and Strategic Thermal Labs transactions. In combination those deals widened Vertiv's reach from coolant distribution and chillers to fluid-management services, heat rejection, and cold-plate design and validation. [CoolTera](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2023/Vertiv-Acquisition-of-CoolTera-Ltd.-Boosts-Liquid-Cooling-Portfolio/default.aspx) [BSE acquisition](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2024/Vertiv-Acquires-Centrifugal-Chiller-Technology-to-Broaden-its-Global-Solutions-Portfolio-in-Support-of-High-Performance-Compute-and-AI/default.aspx) [PurgeRite completion](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2025/Vertiv-Completes-Acquisition-of-PurgeRite-Expanding-Leadership-in-Liquid-Cooling-Services/default.aspx) [ThermoKey announcement](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2026/Vertiv-to-Acquire-ThermoKey-Expanding-Heat-Rejection-Portfolio-for-Converged-Physical-Infrastructure/default.aspx) [Strategic Thermal Labs acquisition](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2026/Vertiv-Strengthens-Liquid-Cooling-System-Capability-with-Acquisition-of-Strategic-Thermal-Labs/)

## Can the Pure-Play Premium Sustain?

| Competitor | Thermal (rack-level) | Thermal (facility) | Power (UPS/PDU) | Services | 2024 Rev (approx.) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vertiv | ✓✓ (CDUs, manifolds, thermal-chain additions) | ✓ | ✓✓ | ✓✓ | ~$8.0B |
| Schneider Electric | ✓✓ | ✓✓ | ✓✓ | ✓✓ | ~€36B (total) |
| Eaton | — | — | ✓✓ | ✓ | ~$24B (total) |
| Trane Technologies | — | ✓✓ | — | ✓ | ~$20B (total) |
| Munters | — | ✓ (evap.) | — | ✓ | ~SEK 15B |
| Asetek | ✓ (cold plate) | — | — | limited | <$100M |

The table above flattens a more textured reality, but the strategic read is clear: within the mission-critical data centre infrastructure market, only Schneider Electric matches Vertiv's breadth across thermal and power at both the rack and facility layers. The conglomerates — Eaton, Trane, ABB — are partial competitors at best, with meaningful overlap in one product dimension but not the integrated thermal-plus-power stack that hyperscaler and colocation procurement teams increasingly prefer.

The 2026 additions were especially notable because they attacked remaining gaps around heat rejection and server-side liquid-cooling validation rather than merely adding volume. ThermoKey brought dry coolers and microchannel heat-exchange technologies; Strategic Thermal Labs added cold-plate design, server-side liquid cooling and high-density thermal validation. The strategic question nevertheless stayed the same: whether Vertiv's systems-level breadth would prove durable enough to withstand Schneider's balance sheet and the specialists' speed. [ThermoKey announcement](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2026/Vertiv-to-Acquire-ThermoKey-Expanding-Heat-Rejection-Portfolio-for-Converged-Physical-Infrastructure/default.aspx) [Strategic Thermal Labs acquisition](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2026/Vertiv-Strengthens-Liquid-Cooling-System-Capability-with-Acquisition-of-Strategic-Thermal-Labs/)

Whether the margin trajectory continues depends in part on whether integrated platform breadth or specialist depth wins the next generation of data-center infrastructure contracting cycles, and whether Vertiv's cooling-plus-power integration can remain differentiated as Schneider and the thermal specialists invest their own capital to converge on the same architectural answer.

chapters.title: From the 2020 SPAC to the 2024 AI inflection and CoolIT
chapters.body:
## The Catalyst Timeline

This chapter focuses on disclosed events and filings rather than the noisier sell-side or social-media layer. The key correction is simple: official Vertiv disclosures through May 23, 2026 did not show a CoolIT transaction. The thermal M&A cadence that mattered instead ran through CoolTera, BSE, Great Lakes, PurgeRite, ThermoKey and Strategic Thermal Labs. [CoolTera](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2023/Vertiv-Acquisition-of-CoolTera-Ltd.-Boosts-Liquid-Cooling-Portfolio/default.aspx) [BSE acquisition](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2024/Vertiv-Acquires-Centrifugal-Chiller-Technology-to-Broaden-its-Global-Solutions-Portfolio-in-Support-of-High-Performance-Compute-and-AI/default.aspx) [Great Lakes completion](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2025/Vertiv-Completes-Acquisition-of-Great-Lakes-Data-Racks--Cabinets/default.aspx) [PurgeRite completion](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2025/Vertiv-Completes-Acquisition-of-PurgeRite-Expanding-Leadership-in-Liquid-Cooling-Services/default.aspx) [ThermoKey announcement](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2026/Vertiv-to-Acquire-ThermoKey-Expanding-Heat-Rejection-Portfolio-for-Converged-Physical-Infrastructure/default.aspx) [Strategic Thermal Labs acquisition](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2026/Vertiv-Strengthens-Liquid-Cooling-System-Capability-with-Acquisition-of-Strategic-Thermal-Labs/)

## The November 2022 Inflection

The timing of the January 2023 CEO succession proved significant because the post-ChatGPT AI buildout pushed infrastructure design conversations upstream. Vertiv's fourth-quarter 2023 release already showed record backlog of $5.5 billion, 23% organic orders growth and a 1.3x book-to-bill ratio, while management explicitly tied the opportunity set to AI demand and the CoolTera transaction completed that December. [Q4 2023 earnings release](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1674101/000162828024005765/exhibit991vrt02212024.htm) [CoolTera](https://investors.vertiv.com/news/news-details/2023/Vertiv-Acquisition-of-CoolTera-Ltd.-Boosts-Liquid-Cooling-Portfolio/default.aspx)

## 2024: Product cadence turned the thesis tangible

The important 2024 catalyst sequence was product and capacity disclosure, not rhetoric. In April Vertiv launched 360AI and, in the same first-quarter release, reported 60% organic orders growth and a 1.5x book-to-bill ratio. In July it launched MegaMod CoolChip and said prefabrication could cut deployment time by up to 50%. In October it introduced the CoolPhase CDU and CoolChip Fluid Network for direct-to-chip deployments in facilities without chilled-water plants.
